_comment: One agent's INSPECTION of every extracted image and every vector-figure render in this library, as data rather than code, so the judgement can be reviewed line by line and re-run (bean d5f1; vector renders, bean ay3x). `saw` is the REASON for the role, not the description; `draft` is the description. Every entry was produced by looking at the image or render file; where a thumbnail's text was too small to read, the draft says so rather than guessing. Applied by cat-harness-tools/scripts/apply-image-verdicts.ts, which writes an `inspection` basis naming this agent and leaves every narrative in `draft` -- only a human may confirm one (schemas/narrative.ts). No person has reviewed these drafts. The model is recorded as `not-disclosed` with the session it can be recovered from (schemas/attribution.ts, MODEL_NOT_DISCLOSED).

img-p011-1.saw: Figure 1, a pie of five segments around a central circle
img-p011-1.draft: Figure 1, 'Elements of a strong catch-up vaccination strategy'. A circle divided into five coloured segments around a central circle labelled 'Catch-up vaccination policy and schedule'. The segments, clockwise from the top right, are: vaccines and supplies for catch-up vaccination; health worker knowledge and practice; recording and reporting practices, information systems and tools; communications and community engagement to build support; and strategies for catch-up vaccination.

img-p034-1.saw: a table of minimum intervals between DTP-containing doses by age group
img-p034-1.draft: A table headed 'Minimum interval from the most recent dose administered'. Rows give the age-appropriate vaccine: 1-4 years, DTwP, DTaP or DT; 4-7 years, DTwP, DTaP, Td or DT; over 7 years, Td or TdaP. Columns give the dose, with the same interval for all three rows: 1st dose as early as possible; 2nd dose at least 4 weeks after the 1st; 3rd dose at least 6 months after the 2nd; 4th dose at least 1 year after the 3rd; 5th dose at least 1 year after the 4th.

img-p038-1.saw: an 'Instructions' panel of three steps with two cartoon children
img-p038-1.draft: An 'Instructions' panel of three steps for the health worker. Step 1: praise the parent or caregiver for bringing the child, and find out from the immunization record or caregiver how old the child is today and which vaccines the child has already received. Step 2: use the chart to the right to decide what to give; the child should already have received all vaccines due up to their current age, and if doses are missing it is not too late; administer the vaccines for which the child is eligible, respecting the necessary spacing. Step 3: remind the caregiver when to bring the child back for subsequent doses and emphasise the importance of completing the series. Cartoon drawings of a standing girl and a seated baby decorate the panel.

img-p039-1.saw: the 'Which vaccines can be given today?' chart of vaccine columns against age rows
img-p039-1.draft: A chart titled 'Which vaccines can be given today?', with the line 'It is better to vaccinate late than never!'. Rows are ages (birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 9 months, 18 months, 2 years); coloured columns are vaccines, each starting at the age of its first dose and running downward as an arrow. HepB BD and BCG start at birth, HepB BD ending at a stop sign; OPV 1-3, PCV 1-3, Penta 1-3 and RV 1-3 at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, RV ending at a stop sign before 2 years; IPV at 14 weeks; MCV 1 at 9 months; DTP4 (or Penta4), MCV 2 and MenA at 18 months. A 'When to give' column gives the timing for each row (for example, at 10 weeks or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after dose 1), and a 'When not to give' column gives the limits: HepB BD not after 6 weeks; RV1, RV2 and RV3 not after 2 years of age; later doses not before 4 weeks since the previous dose; MCV1 and MenA not before 9 months of age except where indicated. A footer says there is no need to restart a series after a long gap, and there is no upper age limit for most vaccines except rotavirus (under 2 years) and the hepatitis B birth dose (under 6 weeks).

A footnote marks Rota 3, DTP4/Other and the net as depending on national health priorities and schedule of services.

vfig-p013.saw: Fig. 1, health content plus digital health interventions plus digital applications, above a foundational-layer grid
vfig-p013.draft: Fig. 1, 'Digital adaptation kits representing health content within broader needs for digital health implementations'. Three boxes are joined by plus signs: HEALTH CONTENT (information aligned with recommended health practices or validated health content), shown with the cover of this kit; DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS (a discrete function of digital technology to achieve health-sector objectives); and DIGITAL APPLICATIONS (ICT systems and communication channels that facilitate delivery of the interventions and content). An orange frame encloses the three, and dotted lines run from it to the highlighted 'Services and applications' cell of a Foundational Layer (ICT and enabling environment) below, whose other cells are leadership and governance, strategy and investment, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation, policy and compliance, and workforce. Source: adapted from reference 14.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 2, the five SMART layers L1-L5 on the left, each feeding a country L1-L5 adaptation on the right through a localisation bar
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 2, 'Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum'. Five rows: L1 Narrative (narrative guidelines: evidence-based recommendations with implementation and data guidance); L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits: software-neutral documentation of operational and functional requirements such as personas, workflows, metadata, algorithms, minimum data sets and priority metrics); L3 Machine readable (structured software-neutral specifications, code, terminology and interoperability standards); L4 Executable (reference software that executes static algorithms and interoperable components); and L5 Dynamic (precision health models trained and optimised with advanced analytics). Each row passes through a vertical 'Localisation' bar to its country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures; localised requirements; localised machine-readable code and standards; localised static digital services within a digital health enterprise; and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. A blue arrow beside them runs from 'Paper systems' at the top to 'Smart digital systems' at the bottom. Source: adapted from reference 18.

vfig-p024.saw: Fig. 3, seven coloured phases with their steps, beside a grid of resource tiles
vfig-p024.draft: Fig. 3, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases, each with its steps: 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling. Beside them a grid of tiles names resources for each phase, marked as PDF for print or online environment; among them the WHO-ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), WHO guideline recommendations on digital interventions, Open Health Information Exchange, TOGAF, and a highlighted tile 'WHO SMART guidelines: digital adaptation kits (this document) and machine-readable recommendations' in phase 05. Source: adapted from WHO (reference 1).

vfig-p040.saw: Fig. 4, a two-lane process overview of workflows A-I
vfig-p040.draft: Fig. 4, 'Overview of key immunization processes'. Two swimlanes. Vaccination location management holds A. vaccination location registration, G. resolve duplicate client records, H. resolve duplicate vaccination events, I. report generation, and a grey 'Supply chain management' box not covered by this kit. Vaccination location runs from Start through B. plan service delivery into a Service Delivery area: C. client registration, D. administer vaccine, then 'All vaccine series complete?'; yes ends the process, no leads to E. client reminder and 'Overdue for a dose?', where yes leads to F. defaulter tracing and no to the end. Each workflow box carries a subprocess marker.

vfig-p046.draft: Fig. 6, 'Workflow B: plan service delivery business process', in one lane (vaccination location, health worker). vfig-p058.saw: Fig. 9, a two-lane reminder process between the immunization registry and the health worker
vfig-p058.draft: Fig. 9, 'Workflow E: client reminder business process'. Two lanes: electronic immunization registry, and vaccination location health worker. From Start the health worker does 1. define/evaluate criteria and 2. select notification method; the registry does 3. generate list of clients and 4. send notifications. Then 5. client shows up for vaccination? Yes leads to D. administer vaccine; no leads to 6. is another reminder needed? Yes loops back to step 1; no leads to F. defaulter tracing.

vfig-p064.saw: Fig. 11, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate client records
vfig-p064.draft: Fig. 11, 'Workflow G: resolve duplicate client records business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. flag client records for evaluation and 2. produce list of potential duplicate records; the person does 3. perform manual review and decides 4. can records be merged? Yes leads to 5. merge records in the PCPOSS; no leads to 6. mark as 'not a duplicate' or 'pending'. Both end the process.

vfig-p066.saw: Fig. 12, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate vaccination events
vfig-p066.draft: Fig. 12, 'Workflow H: resolve duplicate vaccination events business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. identify groups of vaccination events for evaluation; the person does 2. evaluate vaccination event records and decides 3. duplicate events? No ends the process; yes leads to 4. select the most accurate/suitable event record, then the PCPOSS does 5. update vaccination event records and 6. generate report of duplicate vaccination events, and the process ends.

vfig-p068.saw: Fig. 13, a two-lane process for generating reports
vfig-p068.draft: Fig. 13, 'Workflow I: report generation business process'. Two lanes: vaccination location health worker, and PCPOSS. From Start the health worker does 1. define parameters for report; the PCPOSS does 2. generate report; the health worker does 3. high level review and decides 4. report acceptable? No loops back to step 1; yes leads to 5. analyse, and the process ends.

vfig-p036.saw: Figure 3, a four-lane Continuity of Care workflow with every path shown
vfig-p036.draft: Figure 3, 'Continuity of Care scenario': the vaccine is administered, the core data set is recorded on the DDCC paper certificate, and the record is then made available in digital form. Four lanes: subject of care, vaccinator, data entry personnel, DDCC holder. (1) The subject of care arrives at the care site; (2) the vaccinator vaccinates and (3) records core data set elements on a paper certificate, which the holder receives as Point A, a paper record of DDCC:VS. Is there a digital health solution at the care site? If no, (5) data entry personnel record the elements in a digital health solution. If yes, (4) the vaccinator records them in one; then, does the care site have Internet connectivity? Yes leads directly, and no via step 5, to Point B: the record of vaccination status is available in a digital form. End.

vfig-p038.saw: Figure 4, the Figure 3 workflow with the Paper First path highlighted and the rest greyed
vfig-p038.draft: Figure 4, 'Continuity of Care scenario: Paper First use case (UC001)'. The Figure 3 workflow with one path highlighted: arrival (1), vaccination (2), recording on the paper certificate (3) which gives Point A, then no digital health solution at the care site, so data entry personnel record the data in a digital health solution (5), reaching Point B, the record available in digital form. Step 4 and the connectivity decision are greyed out.

vfig-p046.saw: Figure 7, five services joined by labelled arrows, some dashed and optional
vfig-p046.draft: Figure 7, 'The relationships between digital services for Proof of Vaccination'. A digital health solution submits a vaccination event to the DDCC:VS generation service, which returns a DDCC:VS. The HCID is provided by an existing national system or issued by the generation service. The generation service registers the DDCC:VS with the DDCC:VS registry service and may optionally store it in a DDCC:VS repository. Optional dashed links: an online status check between the registry service and the repository, and online verification of a DDCC:VS between an optional status checking application and the registry service. A note explains that the HCID, the unique identifier in a DDCC:VS, is used throughout these services and lets verifiers search for and retrieve a DDCC:VS.

vfig-p048.saw: Figure 8, a four-lane Proof of Vaccination workflow with every path shown
vfig-p048.draft: Figure 8, 'Proof of Vaccination scenario': verification of a claim of vaccination. Four lanes: DDCC holder, verifier, national PHA, international PHA. (1) The holder presents the DDCC:VS; (2) the verifier receives the claim. Is cryptographic verification required? No leads straight to Point C, the decision on the verification. Yes: (3) the verifier uses a status checking application; perform check online? No leads to Point C. Yes: (4) the national PHA performs an online check with its DDCC registry service; check with international PHA? If yes, (5) the international PHA performs an online check with its registry service; either way (6) results are communicated back to the verifier, then Point C and End.

vfig-p064.saw: Figure 13, three certificate boxes with a numbered signing arc above and a dotted verifying arc below
vfig-p064.draft: Figure 13, 'The chain of trust'. Three linked boxes: CSCA (country signing certificate authority) and DSC (document signer certificate), each with a private and a public key, and DDCC (Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificate), marked with a QR code. Above, 'Signing and issuing a DDCC' runs in steps 1-3 from CSCA through DSC to DDCC. Below, a dotted 'Verifying a DDCC' arc runs in steps 1-3 the other way, from DDCC back to CSCA.

vfig-p065.draft: Figure 14, 'How digital signatures work', under the heading Document Signing. A signer starts from a document (vaccination data); a hash is calculated from the document, giving the document hash; the hash is digitally signed with a private key, giving the signed hash; the signed hash is added to the document, giving a document with a digitally signed hash (the DDCC:VS).

vfig-p066.saw: Figure 15, the signing flow above a validation flow
vfig-p066.draft: Figure 15, 'How digital signature verification works'. The upper panel, Document Signing, repeats Figure 14: document, document hash, signed with the private key, signed hash added to the document to make the DDCC:VS. The signer sends the digitally signed document and the public key to the verifier. The lower panel, Document Validation: the verifier calculates a hash from the document and, using the public key, obtains the hash from the signed hash; the two values are compared, and a matching hash indicates a valid document, one that contains the information that was signed with the private key.
